=== Number of solutions ===

[[File:Apollonius no solutions black.svg|thumb|right|Figure 11: An Apollonius problem with no solutions. A solution circle (pink) must cross the dashed given circle (black) to touch both of the other given circles (also black).]]

The problem of counting the number of solutions to different types of Apollonius's problem belongs to the field of [[enumerative geometry]].<ref name="bruen_1983"/><ref name="dreschler sterz">{{cite journal|journal=Acta Mathematica Universitatis Comenianae|volume=68|issue=1|year=1999|pages=37–47|title=Apollonius' contact problem in ''n''-space in view of enumerative geometry|vauthors=Dreschler K, Sterz U |url=http://www.emis.de/journals/AMUC/_vol-68/_no_1/_drechsl/drechsle.html}}</ref> The general number of solutions for each of the ten types of Apollonius's problem is given in Table&nbsp;1 above. However, special arrangements of the given elements may change the number of solutions. For illustration, Apollonius's problem has no solution if one circle separates the two (Figure&nbsp;11); to touch both the solid given circles, the solution circle would have to cross the dashed given circle; but that it cannot do, if it is to touch the dashed circle tangentially. Conversely, if three given circles are all tangent at the same point, then ''any'' circle tangent at the same point is a solution; such Apollonius problems have an infinite number of solutions. If any of the given circles are identical, there is likewise an infinity of solutions. If only two given circles are identical, there are only two distinct given circles; the centers of the solution circles form a [[hyperbola]], as used in [[#Intersecting hyperbolas|one solution]] to Apollonius's problem.

An exhaustive enumeration of the number of solutions for all possible configurations of three given circles, points or lines was first undertaken by Muirhead in 1896,<ref name="muirhead_1896" >{{cite journal| author = Muirhead RF| year = 1896| title = On the Number and nature of the Solutions of the Apollonian Contact Problem| journal = Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society| volume = 14| pages = 135–147, attached figures 44–114| doi = 10.1017/S0013091500031898| doi-access = free}}</ref> although earlier work had been done by Stoll<ref name="stoll_1876">{{cite journal| author = Stoll V| year = 1876| title = Zum Problem des Apollonius| journal = Mathematische Annalen| volume = 6| pages = 613–632| doi = 10.1007/BF01443201| issue = 4| s2cid = 120097802| url = https://zenodo.org/record/2212775|language=de}}</ref> and Study.<ref name="study_1897">{{cite journal| author = Study E| year = 1897| title = Das Apollonische Problem| journal = Mathematische Annalen| volume = 49| pages = 497–542| doi = 10.1007/BF01444366| issue = 3–4| s2cid = 120984176|language=de}}</ref> However, Muirhead's work was incomplete; it was extended in 1974<ref name="fitzgerald_1974">{{cite journal| author = Fitz-Gerald JM| year = 1974| title = A Note on a Problem of Apollonius| journal = Journal of Geometry| volume = 5| pages = 15–26| doi = 10.1007/BF01954533| s2cid = 59444157}}</ref> and a definitive enumeration, with 33 distinct cases, was published in 1983.<ref name="bruen_1983">{{cite journal|vauthors=Bruen A, Fisher JC, Wilker JB | year = 1983| title = Apollonius by Inversion| journal = Mathematics Magazine| volume = 56| pages = 97–103| doi = 10.2307/2690380| jstor = 2690380| issue = 2}}</ref> Although solutions to Apollonius's problem generally occur in pairs related by [[#Pairs of solutions by inversion|inversion]], an odd number of solutions is possible in some cases, e.g., the single solution for '''PPP''', or when one or three of the given circles are themselves solutions. (An example of the latter is given in the [[#Mutually tangent given circles: Soddy's circles and Descartes's theorem|section]] on [[Descartes's theorem]].) However, there are no Apollonius problems with seven solutions.<ref name="pedoe_1970" /><ref name="stoll_1876" /> Alternative solutions based on the [[Lie sphere geometry|geometry of circles and spheres]] have been developed and used in higher dimensions.<ref name="zlobec_2001" /><ref name="knight_2005">{{cite journal| author = Knight RD| year = 2005| title = The Apollonius contact problem and Lie contact geometry| journal = Journal of Geometry| volume = 83| issue = 1–2| pages = 137–152| doi = 10.1007/s00022-005-0009-x| s2cid = 122228528}}</ref>

=== Mutually tangent given circles: Soddy's circles and Descartes's theorem ===

If the three given circles are mutually tangent, Apollonius's problem has five solutions. Three solutions are the given circles themselves, since each is tangent to itself and to the other two given circles. The remaining two solutions (shown in red in Figure&nbsp;12) correspond to the [[incircle and excircles of a triangle|inscribed]] and [[circumscribed circle]]s, and are called ''Soddy's circles''.<ref>{{cite journal| author = Eppstein D| author-link = David Eppstein| date=1 January 2001| title = Tangent Spheres and Triangle Centers| journal = The American Mathematical Monthly| volume = 108| pages = 63–66| doi = 10.2307/2695679| issn = 0002-9890| issue = 1| jstor = 2695679| arxiv = math/9909152| s2cid=14002377}}</ref> This special case of Apollonius's problem is also known as the '''four coins problem'''.<ref>{{cite journal| author = Oldknow A| date=1 April 1996| title = The Euler–Gergonne–Soddy Triangle of a Triangle| journal = The American Mathematical Monthly| volume = 103| pages = 319–329| doi = 10.2307/2975188| issn = 0002-9890| issue = 4| jstor = 2975188}}<br/>
{{cite web|author-link= Eric W. Weisstein|author= Weisstein, EW| title = Four Coins Problem| url = http://mathworld.wolfram.com/FourCoinsProblem.html| publisher = [[MathWorld]]| access-date = 2008-10-06}}</ref> The three given circles of this Apollonius problem form a [[Steiner chain]] tangent to the two Soddy's circles.

[[File:DescartesCircles.svg|thumb|left|Figure 12: The two solutions (red) to Apollonius's problem with mutually tangent given circles (black), labeled by their curvatures.]]

Either Soddy circle, when taken together with the three given circles, produces a set of four circles that are mutually tangent at six points. The radii of these four circles are related by an equation known as [[Descartes's theorem]]. In a 1643 letter to Princess [[Elizabeth of Bohemia]],<ref>[[René Descartes|Descartes R]], ''Œuvres de Descartes, Correspondance IV'', (C. Adam and P. Tannery, Eds.), Paris: Leopold Cert 1901. {{in lang|fr}}</ref> [[René Descartes]] showed that

: <math>
(k_1+k_2+k_3+k_s)^2 = 2( k_1^2 + k_2^2 + k_3^2 + k_s^2)
</math>

where ''k''<sub>''s''</sub> = 1/''r''<sub>''s''</sub> and ''r''<sub>''s''</sub> are the [[curvature]] and radius of the solution circle, respectively, and similarly for the curvatures ''k''<sub>1</sub>, ''k''<sub>2</sub> and ''k''<sub>3</sub> and radii ''r''<sub>1</sub>, ''r''<sub>2</sub> and ''r''<sub>3</sub> of the three given circles. For every set of four mutually tangent circles, there is a second set of four mutually tangent circles that are tangent at the same six points.<ref name="coxeter_1968" /><ref name="beecroft_1842" />

{{anchor|kiss_precise}}Descartes's theorem was rediscovered independently in 1826 by [[Jakob Steiner]],<ref name="steiner_1826" >{{cite journal| author = Steiner J| author-link = Jakob Steiner| year = 1826| title = Einige geometrische Betrachtungen| journal = Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik| volume = 1| pages = [https://www.degruyter.com/view/journals/crll/1826/1/article-p161.xml 161–184], [https://www.degruyter.com/view/journals/crll/1826/1/article-p252.xml 252–288]| doi = 10.1515/crll.1826.1.161| s2cid = 122065577| url = https://zenodo.org/record/1919411}}</ref> in 1842 by Philip Beecroft,<ref name="coxeter_1968" /><ref name="beecroft_1842">{{cite journal| author = Beecroft H| year = 1842| title = Properties of Circles in Mutual Contact| journal =[[The Lady's and Gentleman's Diary]]| volume = 139| pages = 91–96}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Beecroft H| year = 1846| title = Unknown title| journal =[[The Lady's and Gentleman's Diary]]| page = 51}} ({{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20080118112427/http://www.pballew.net/soddy.html MathWords online article]}})</ref> and again in 1936 by [[Frederick Soddy]].<ref name="soddy_1936" >{{cite journal| author = Soddy F| author-link = Frederick Soddy| date = 20 June 1936| title = The Kiss Precise| journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]| volume = 137| page = 1021| doi = 10.1038/1371021a0| issue=3477| bibcode = 1936Natur.137.1021S| doi-access = free}}</ref> Soddy published his findings in the scientific journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' as a poem, ''The Kiss Precise'', of which the first two stanzas are reproduced below. The first stanza describes Soddy's circles, whereas the second stanza gives Descartes's theorem. In Soddy's poem, two circles are said to "kiss" if they are tangent, whereas the term "bend" refers to the curvature ''k'' of the circle.

{{col-float
|style=font-style: italic; width: 18em; margin-left: 1.6em;
|1=
<poem>For pairs of lips to kiss maybe
Involves no trigonometry.
'Tis not so when four circles kiss
Each one the other three.
To bring this off the four must be
As three in one or one in three.
If one in three, beyond a doubt
Each gets three kisses from without.
If three in one, then is that one
Thrice kissed internally.
</poem>
|2=
<poem>Four circles to the kissing come.
The smaller are the benter.
The bend is just the inverse of
The distance from the center.
Though their intrigue left Euclid dumb
There's now no need for rule of thumb.
Since zero bend's a dead straight line
And concave bends have minus sign,
The sum of the squares of all four bends
Is half the square of their sum.
</poem>
}}

Sundry extensions of Descartes's theorem have been derived by [[Daniel Pedoe]].<ref name="pedoe_1967">{{cite journal| author = Pedoe D| author-link = Daniel Pedoe| date=1 June 1967| title = On a theorem in geometry| journal = Amer. Math. Monthly| volume = 74| pages = 627–640| doi = 10.2307/2314247| issn = 0002-9890| issue = 6| jstor = 2314247}}</ref>

== Generalizations ==

Apollonius's problem can be extended to construct all the circles that intersect three given circles at a precise angle θ, or at three specified crossing angles θ<sub>1</sub>, θ<sub>2</sub> and θ<sub>3</sub>;<ref name="steiner_1826" /> the ordinary Apollonius's problem corresponds to a special case in which the crossing angle is zero for all three given circles. Another generalization is the [[duality (mathematics)|dual]] of the first extension, namely, to construct circles with three specified tangential distances from the three given circles.<ref name="zlobec_2001" />

[[File:Apollonian gasket.svg|thumb|left|Figure 13: A symmetrical Apollonian gasket, also called the Leibniz packing, after its inventor [[Gottfried Leibniz]].]]

Apollonius's problem can be extended from the plane to the [[sphere]] and other [[quadric surface|quadratic surfaces]]. For the sphere, the problem is to construct all the circles (the boundaries of [[spherical cap]]s) that are tangent to three given circles on the sphere.<ref name="gergonne_1814" /><ref name="carnot_1803b" >{{cite book| author = Carnot L| author-link = Lazare Carnot| year = 1803| title = Géométrie de position| publisher = Unknown publisher| location = Paris| pages = 415, §356}}</ref><ref name="vanson_1855" >{{cite journal| author = Vannson| year = 1855| title = Contact des cercles sur la sphère, par la geométrie| journal = [[Nouvelles Annales de Mathématiques]]| volume = XIV| pages = 55–71|language=fr}}</ref> This spherical problem can be rendered into a corresponding planar problem using [[stereographic projection]]. Once the solutions to the planar problem have been constructed, the corresponding solutions to the spherical problem can be determined by inverting the stereographic projection. Even more generally, one can consider the problem of four tangent curves that result from the intersections of an arbitrary quadratic surface and four planes, a problem first considered by [[Charles Dupin]].<ref name="altshiller-court_1961" />

By solving Apollonius's problem repeatedly to find the inscribed circle, the interstices between mutually tangential circles can be filled arbitrarily finely, forming an [[Apollonian gasket]], also known as a ''Leibniz packing'' or an ''Apollonian packing''.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Kasner E, Supnick F |date=December 1943| title = The Apollonian Packing of Circles| journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA| volume = 29| pages = 378–384| doi = 10.1073/pnas.29.11.378| pmid = 16588629| issue = 11| issn = 0027-8424| pmc = 1078636|bibcode=1943PNAS...29..378K|doi-access=free}}</ref> This gasket is a [[fractal]], being self-similar and having a [[Hausdorff dimension|dimension]] ''d'' that is not known exactly but is roughly 1.3,<ref name="boyd_1973">{{cite journal| last1=Boyd | first1=David W.| year = 1973| title = Improved Bounds for the Disk Packing Constants| journal = [[Aequationes Mathematicae]]| volume = 9| pages = 99–106| doi = 10.1007/BF01838194| s2cid = 121089590}}<br/>{{cite journal| last1=Boyd | first1=David W.| year = 1973| title = The Residual Set Dimension of the Apollonian Packing| journal = [[Mathematika]]| volume = 20| pages = 170–174| doi = 10.1112/S0025579300004745| issue = 2}}<br/>{{cite journal|last=McMullen|first=Curtis T. |title= Hausdorff dimension and conformal dynamics III: Computation of dimension|url=http://abel.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/papers/home/text/papers/dimIII/dimIII.pdf|journal=American Journal of Mathematics|volume=120|year=1998|pages=691–721|doi=10.1353/ajm.1998.0031|issue=4|s2cid= 15928775}}</ref> which is higher than that of a [[regular curve|regular]] (or [[rectifiable curve|rectifiable]]) curve (''d'' = 1) but less than that of a plane (''d'' = 2). The Apollonian gasket was first described by [[Gottfried Leibniz]] in the 17th century, and is a curved precursor of the 20th-century [[Sierpiński triangle]].<ref>{{cite book| author = Mandelbrot B| author-link = Benoit Mandelbrot| year = 1983| title = The Fractal Geometry of Nature| publisher = W. H. Freeman| location = New York| isbn = 978-0-7167-1186-5| page = [https://archive.org/details/fractalgeometryo00beno/page/170 170]| url = https://archive.org/details/fractalgeometryo00beno/page/170}}<br/>{{cite book| vauthors = Aste T, Weaire D| author2-link = Denis Weaire| year = 2008| title = The Pursuit of Perfect Packing |title-link=The Pursuit of Perfect Packing| edition = 2nd| publisher = Taylor and Francis| location = New York| isbn = 978-1-4200-6817-7| pages = 131–138}}</ref> The Apollonian gasket also has deep connections to other fields of mathematics; for example, it is the limit set of [[Kleinian group]]s.<ref>{{cite book| vauthors = Mumford D, Series C, Wright D| author-link = David Mumford| year = 2002| title = Indra's Pearls: The Vision of Felix Klein| url = https://archive.org/details/indraspearlsvisi00mumf| url-access = limited| publisher = Cambridge University Press| location = Cambridge| isbn = 0-521-35253-3| pages = [https://archive.org/details/indraspearlsvisi00mumf/page/n213 196]–223}}</ref>

The configuration of a circle tangent to ''four'' circles in the plane has special properties, which have been elucidated by Larmor (1891)<ref name="larmor_1891">{{cite journal| author = Larmor A| year = 1891| title = Contacts of Systems of Circles| journal = Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society| volume = 23| pages = 136–157| doi = 10.1112/plms/s1-23.1.135| url = https://zenodo.org/record/1447730}}</ref> and Lachlan (1893).<ref name="lachlan_1893">{{cite book| author = Lachlan R| year = 1893| title = An elementary treatise on modern pure geometry| publisher = Macmillan| location = London| pages = §383–396, pp. 244–251}} {{ isbn | 1-4297-0050-5}}.</ref> Such a configuration is also the basis for [[Casey's theorem]],<ref name="casey_1881" /> itself a generalization of [[Ptolemy's theorem]].<ref name="johnson_1929" />

The extension of Apollonius's problem to three dimensions, namely, the problem of finding a fifth sphere that is tangent to four given spheres, can be solved by analogous methods.<ref name="altshiller-court_1961" /> For example, the given and solution spheres can be resized so that one given sphere is shrunk to point while maintaining tangency.<ref name="ogilvy_1969" /> Inversion in this point reduces Apollonius's problem to finding a plane that is tangent to three given spheres. There are in general eight such planes, which become the solutions to the original problem by reversing the inversion and the resizing. This problem was first considered by [[Pierre de Fermat]],<ref>[[Pierre de Fermat|de Fermat P]], ''Varia opera mathematica'', p. 74, Tolos, 1679.</ref> and many alternative solution methods have been developed over the centuries.<ref name="fermat_problem_solutions" >{{cite journal| author = Euler L| author-link = Leonhard Euler| year = 1810| title = Solutio facilis problematis, quo quaeritur sphaera, quae datas quatuor sphaeras utcunque dispositas contingat| journal = Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences de St.-Pétersbourg| volume = 2| pages = 17–28| url = http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~euler/docs/originals/E733.pdf| language = la}} Reprinted in Euler's ''Opera Omnia'', series 1, volume 26, pp. 334–343.<br/>{{cite book| author = Carnot L| author-link = Lazare Carnot| year = 1803| title = Géométrie de position| url = https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_EJx6U7IW_iEC| publisher = Imprimerie de Crapelet, chez J. B. M. Duprat| location = Paris| pages = [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_EJx6U7IW_iEC/page/n382 357], §416| language = fr}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Hachette JNP| author-link = Jean Nicolas Pierre Hachette|date=September 1808| title = Sur le contact des sphères; sur la sphère tangente à quatre sphères données; sur le cercle tangent à trois cercles donnés| journal = Correspondance sur l'École Polytechnique| volume = 1| issue = 2| pages = 27–28|language=fr}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Français J|date=January 1810| title = De la sphère tangente à quatre sphères données| journal = Correspondance sur l'École Impériale Polytechnique| volume = 2| issue = 2| pages = 63–66|language=fr}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Français J|date=January 1813| title = Solution analytique du problème de la sphère tangente à quatre sphères données| journal = Correspondance sur l'École Impériale Polytechnique| volume = 2| issue = 5| pages = 409–410|language=fr}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Dupin C| author-link = Charles Dupin|date=January 1813| title = Mémoire sur les sphères| journal = Correspondance sur l'École Impériale Polytechnique| volume = 2| issue = 5| page = 423|language=fr}}<br/>{{cite book| author = Reye T| year = 1879| title = Synthetische Geometrie der Kugeln| publisher = B. G. Teubner| location = Leipzig| url = http://www.gutenberg.org/files/17153/17153-pdf.pdf| language = de}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Serret JA| author-link = Joseph Alfred Serret| year = 1848| title = De la sphère tangente à quatre sphères donnèes| journal = Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik| volume = 1848| issue = 37| pages = 51–57| doi = 10.1515/crelle-1848-18483704| s2cid = 201061558| url = https://zenodo.org/record/2171705}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Coaklay GW| date = 1859–1860| title = Analytical Solutions of the Ten Problems in the Tangencies of Circles; and also of the Fifteen Problems in the Tangencies of Spheres| journal = The Mathematical Monthly| volume = 2| pages = 116–126}}<br/>{{cite journal| author = Alvord B| author-link = Benjamin Alvord (mathematician)| date=1 January 1882| title = The intersection of circles and intersection of spheres| journal = American Journal of Mathematics| volume = 5| pages = 25–44, with four pages of Figures| doi = 10.2307/2369532| issn = 0002-9327| issue = 1| jstor = 2369532}}<br/></ref>

Apollonius's problem can even be extended to ''d'' dimensions, to construct the [[hypersphere]]s tangent to a given set of {{nowrap|''d'' + 1}} hyperspheres.<ref name="dreschler sterz"/> Following the publication of [[Frederick Soddy]]'s re-derivation of the [[Descartes's theorem]] in 1936, several people solved (independently) the mutually tangent case corresponding to Soddy's circles in ''d'' dimensions.<ref name="gossett_1937" >{{cite journal| author = Gossett T| year = 1937| title = The Kiss Precise| journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]| volume = 139| page = 62| doi = 10.1038/139062a0| issue=3506| bibcode = 1937Natur.139Q..62.| doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Applications ==

The principal application of Apollonius's problem, as formulated by Isaac Newton, is [[hyperbolic positioning|hyperbolic trilateration]], which seeks to determine a position from the ''differences'' in distances to at least three points.<ref name="Schmidt 1972">{{cite journal| author = Schmidt, RO| year = 1972| title = A new approach to geometry of range difference location| journal = IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems| volume = AES-8| pages = 821–835| doi = 10.1109/TAES.1972.309614| issue = 6| bibcode = 1972ITAES...8..821S| s2cid = 51648067}}</ref> For example, a ship may seek to determine its position from the differences in arrival times of signals from three synchronized transmitters. Solutions to Apollonius's problem were used in [[World War I]] to determine the location of an artillery piece from the time a gunshot was heard at three different positions,<ref name="altshiller-court_1961" /> and hyperbolic trilateration is the principle used by the [[Decca Navigator System]] and [[LORAN]].<ref name="Hofmann-Wellenhof">{{cite book|title=Navigation: Principles of Positioning and Guidance|vauthors=Hofmann-Wellenhof B, Legat K, Wieser M, Lichtenegger H |publisher= Springer|year= 2003|isbn=978-3-211-00828-7}}</ref> Similarly, the location of an aircraft may be determined from the difference in arrival times of its [[transponder (aviation)|transponder]] signal at four receiving stations. This [[multilateration]] problem is equivalent to the three-dimensional generalization of Apollonius's problem and applies to [[global navigation satellite systems]] (see [[GPS#Geometric interpretation]]).<ref name="Hoshen 1996" >{{cite journal| author = Hoshen J| year = 1996| title = The GPS Equations and the Problem of Apollonius| journal = IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems| volume = 32| pages = 1116–1124| doi = 10.1109/7.532270| issue = 3| bibcode = 1996ITAES..32.1116H| s2cid = 30190437}}</ref> It is also used to determine the position of calling animals (such as birds and whales), although Apollonius's problem does not pertain if the [[speed of sound]] varies with direction (i.e., the [[transmission medium]] not [[isotropic]]).<ref name="spiesberger_2004">{{cite journal| author = Spiesberger, JL| year = 2004| title = Geometry of locating sounds from differences in travel time: Isodiachrons| journal = [[Journal of the Acoustical Society of America]] | volume = 116| pages =3168–3177| doi = 10.1121/1.1804625| issue = 5| pmid = 15603162| bibcode = 2004ASAJ..116.3168S| s2cid = 626749| url = https://repository.upenn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1010&context=ees_papers}}</ref>

Apollonius's problem has other applications. In Book 1, Proposition 21 in his ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Principia]]'', [[Isaac Newton]] used his solution of Apollonius's problem to construct an orbit in [[celestial mechanics]] from the center of attraction and observations of tangent lines to the orbit corresponding to instantaneous [[velocity]].<ref name="altshiller-court_1961" /> The special case of the problem of Apollonius when all three circles are tangent is used in the [[Hardy–Littlewood circle method]] of [[analytic number theory]] to construct [[Hans Rademacher]]'s contour for complex integration, given by the boundaries of an [[infinite set]] of [[Ford circle]]s each of which touches several others.<ref>{{cite book| author = Apostol TM| author-link = Tom M. Apostol| title = Modular functions and Dirichlet series in number theory| url = https://archive.org/details/modularfunctions0000apos| url-access = registration| publisher = [[Springer-Verlag]]| location = New York| edition = 2nd| isbn = 978-0-387-97127-8| year = 1990}}</ref> Finally, Apollonius's problem has been applied to some types of [[packing problem]]s, which arise in disparate fields such as the [[error-correcting code]]s used on [[DVD]]s and the design of pharmaceuticals that bind in a particular [[enzyme]] of a pathogenic [[bacteria|bacterium]].<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Lewis RH, Bridgett S | year = 2003| title = Conic Tangency Equations and Apollonius Problems in Biochemistry and Pharmacology| journal = Mathematics and Computers in Simulation| volume = 61| pages = 101–114| doi = 10.1016/S0378-4754(02)00122-2| issue = 2}}</ref>
